title: Can female founders have it all? Motherhood & entrepreneurship
guest: Farah Jesani, CEO and 'Chief Chai Officer' of One Stripe Chai
summary: Farah Jesani tells how a barista summer and an obsession with why nobody selling chai concentrate looked like her turned into One Stripe Chai, now on Erewhon shelves with a food-service-heavy omnichannel model. She shares candid lessons on buying out a cofounder, being dismissed as a brown female founder, naming products in Hindi to mainstream her culture, and regretting not planning a real maternity leave after an emergency C-section.

ideas.idea: If you are going to be really stressed anyway, be stressed about something you deeply care about.
ideas.detail: That feeling, plus curiosity about why an $8-9 almond milk mocha is justified when coffee beans are a commodity, pushed Farah to explore the specialty beverage supply chain instead of waiting for the next corporate bonus.

ideas.idea: Before quitting to start a business, go work the front line of that industry to learn how it actually operates.
ideas.detail: Farah's father, who made his daughters hold mall jobs in high school to understand money, told her to become a barista before opening a coffee shop; she did a barista training program at an old church coffee shop, which is where she discovered chai was served as pre-brewed concentrates and powders.

ideas.idea: Immigrant families with only daughters tend to place different, often positive, expectations on the women, especially the eldest.
ideas.detail: Jean's nascent theory, endorsed by Farah, is that without sons, daughters are pushed toward self-sufficiency and setting an example; Farah's dad wanted them able to take care of themselves if he died early and not take their privilege for granted.

ideas.idea: The idea you cannot stop thinking about is the business worth pursuing, and it need not start as a master plan.
ideas.detail: Farah could not sleep because no chai brand told the story through lived South Asian experience; it started as a side project tinkering on a recipe until customers made it a business, and she went full time in 2018. Jean notes founders usually rewrite history into a five-year plan.

ideas.idea: Getting into a cult-status retailer like Erewhon is a marketing play for brand recognition more than a profit channel.
ideas.detail: Erewhon's margins are squeezed and it goes through a distributor, but shoppers go there for curation and the staff champion brands. Farah applied through the black-box portal, declined the expensive marketing program, and a month later they offered a December end cap with the program thrown in because the product stood on its own.

ideas.idea: Food service is a better channel than grocery retail for a small CPG brand: recurring B2B orders, bulk packaging and no slotting fees or free fills.
ideas.detail: One Stripe Chai is roughly 65-70% food service and retail and about 30% direct-to-consumer; grocery stores charge slotting fees to put you on the shelf, while cafes reorder whenever they run low. The pandemic forced the brand to add DTC with the Chai at Home blend.

ideas.idea: Meet customers where they are and make the packaging educational.
ideas.detail: When customers were stuck at home during COVID, Farah launched at-home blends; every bag teaches a word, such as Chai means tea and Gulab means rose.

ideas.idea: Name products what they actually are in your own language, as with 'Haldi Doodh' instead of 'golden milk', because culture can go mainstream without being translated.
ideas.detail: Farah's analogy: gnocchi is not called potato pillows, and if you can pronounce Timothee Chalamet you can pronounce naan. After launch, non-South Asians adopted the term and other companies started calling their turmeric blends Haldi Doodh; boba went mainstream the same way.

ideas.idea: Founders planning to have a baby should intentionally design a real maternity leave of at least three months with no work.
ideas.detail: Farah answered emails from the hospital after an emergency C-section and still carries trauma and shame from it; she will not have another child unless the business is set up with a trusted leader who can make decisions without deferring to her. Her husband's paternity leave helped but was not the same as taking time herself.

ideas.idea: Owner-operators who 'just do it' themselves build no boundaries, so hire operations help you trust before life forces you to.
ideas.detail: One Stripe Chai made products in house, packed orders and built pallets itself; pregnancy made that impossible and having someone take over operations was essential.

ideas.idea: A cofounder buyout works when you are willing to walk away and put the choice in their court: either you take it on alone or I do.
ideas.detail: Farah, the only one who had invested money, told her cofounder she would take her money off the table if they wanted to run it, otherwise she would buy them out; it closed cleanly in one to two months. Afterward she felt free to launch Chai at Home and Haldi Doodh and finally comfortable as a South Asian woman running a chai company.

ideas.idea: Before a cofounder split, think through your ideal outcome, what you can afford, how far along the business is, and whether you can live without their expertise.
ideas.detail: Farah accepted a likely short-term struggle without her cofounder's skills because a clean break was worth it; she hopes never to repeat the process.

ideas.idea: Female and brown founders are routinely not taken seriously, and the right response is to call it out and treat it as a filter for bad partners.
ideas.detail: A tech investor asked why her husband did not join One Stripe Chai, and a farm manager in India directed every question to her husband despite knowing it was her company. Farah now makes the snarky comment and concludes anyone who cannot see her value will not be part of her journey.

ideas.idea: Representation compounds: seeing founders who look like you shortens the time it takes to believe you can do it.
ideas.detail: Growing up, Indra Nooyi was the one visible South Asian woman CEO; Farah says having no role model is why it took her so long to consider entrepreneurship, and she hopes her daughter Yara grows up seeing running a business as second nature.

ideas.idea: Many immigrant family businesses were startups in everything but name; they were just called small businesses and funded by bank or family loans rather than VC.
ideas.detail: 'Startup' only became a cool word after Farah graduated; her mother once ran a restaurant and her parents were scrappy entrepreneurs without the label.

ideas.idea: Embrace your identity and intersectionality as a brand's biggest differentiator.
ideas.detail: The hosts' first takeaway: competitors' chai concentrates may have been fine products, but they lacked the authentic story customers want to connect with, and Farah's lived heritage set One Stripe Chai apart.
